1.
The present Claim petition arises out of road accident in which Smt. Tara, aged about 38 years suffered fatal injury resulting in her death.

The present claim for compensation is being pursued by Sh. Shiv Kumar as dependent husband of the deceased, one minor son namely Abhishek (aged 09 years) and two minor daughters, namely, Divya Bharti (aged 16 years) and Rinku (aged 13 years).
2.
Brief facts of the case are that on 06.02.2019, at about 1:30 pm, victim Smt Tara (since deceased in the accident) was sitting outside her house near the door.

At that time, a truck, bearing no.
UP61 AT 2711 (hereinafter referred to as "the offending vehicle") came at a high speed, in an uncontrolled, rash and negligent manner and hit the victim.

After striking the victim, the said offending vehicle hit another person, namely, Sita Ram, S/o Late Sh. Balkhera, a child namely Ansh (aged 02 years) who was playing near the site and three buffaloes.
Thereafter, the offending truck hit against an electricity pole.
3. While victim Smt Tara died on the spot, victim Sita Ram succumbed to the injuries and died on his way to the hospital.
Victim Ansh sustained injuries.

Two out of the three buffaloes,
died on the spot.
4. An FIR no. 19/19 dated 06.02.2019, was registered u/s MACT No. 382/19 Shiv Kumar & ors. v. Brajesh Singh & ors.

13. In the instant case, petitioners have examined Smt.
Fulmati Devi as an eye witness who has given contradictory statement regarding her presence at the spot.

She denied that she was riding bicycle at that time.
She has also contradicted the date of seizure of the offending vehicle.

As per testimony of PW1, the driver of the offending vehicle along with the offending vehicle, was apprehended on the spot while the seizure memo relied upon shows the date of seizure as 09.02.2019, at 03:32 p.m.

Further, it is seen that the FIR regarding the accident was lodged on the same day without any inordinate delay.

Learned counsel for insurance company has raised suspicion as to the veracity of claim on the ground that despite alleging that the offending vehicle hit into three individuals, three buffaloes and an electric pole, the mechanical inspection report reveals no damage.
Such doubt appears to be misconceived in as much as the criminal record of the case proves the offending vehicle to have been seized three days after the accident.
As a lay person, PW2 may not have been able to appreciate formal seizure of the vehicle by the police for the purpose of mechanical inspection.
It is possible that by the time the vehicle was seized and sent for mechanical inspection, it may have been got repaired by the respondents.

As such, mere absence of marks of damage on the offending vehicle after three days of the alleged accident,
does not lead to an inference that it did not meet with any accident, particularly where the accident was duly informed and reported to the police on the same day with particulars of such offending vehicle.

As per postmortem report of Smt. Tara Devi, victim suffered antimortem injuries including amputation of both lower limbs from bilateral region with multiple crushed injuries and laceration and crushing of all vital organs.
Postmortem report of victim Sita Ram also reveals death due to multiple crush injuries.
It is further seen that such postmortem report of victim Tara Devi as well as victim Sita Ram reveals similar nature of injuries MACT No. 382/19 Shiv Kumar & ors. v. Brajesh Singh & ors.

The relevant principles for ascertainment of compensation are quoted here under:
 BASIC PRINCIPLES  "9.

The issues to  be determined by the Tribunal to arrive at the loss of  dependency are (i) additions/deductions to be made for  arriving at the income; (ii) the deduction to be made  towards the personal living expenses of the deceased;
 and (iii) the multiplier to be applied with reference of  the age of the deceased.
If these determinants are  standardized, there will be uniformity and consistency  in the decisions.
There will lesser need for detailed  evidence.
It will also be easier for the insurance  companies to settle accident claims without delay.

determine compensation in cases of death, by the  following well settled steps : -
 Step 1 (Ascertaining the multiplicand)
The income of the deceased per annum should be  determined.
Out of the said income a deduction should
be made in regard to the amount which the deceased  would have spent on himself by way of personal and  living expenses.
The balance, which is considered to be  the contribution to the dependent family, constitutes the  multiplicand.
Step 2 (Ascertaining the multiplier)
Having regard to the age of the deceased and period of  active career, the appropriate multiplier should be  selected.
This does not mean ascertaining the number  of years he would have lived or worked but for the  accident.
Having regard to several imponderables in  life and economic factors, a table of multipliers with  reference to the age has been identified by this Court.
The multiplier should be chosen from the said table  with reference to the age of the deceased.
Step 3 (Actual calculation)

The annual contribution to the family (multiplicand)
 when multiplied by such multiplier gives the `loss of  dependency' to the family.
Thereafter, a conventional  amount in the range of Rs. 5,000/- to Rs.10,000/- may  be added as loss of estate.
Where the deceased is  survived by his widow
, another conventional amount in  the range of 5,000/- to 10,000/- should be added under  the head of loss of consortium.
But no amount is to be  awarded under the head of pain, suffering or  hardship caused to the legal heirs of the deceased.
The funeral expenses, cost of transportation of the  body (if incurred) and cost of any medical treatment of  the deceased before death (if incurred) should also  added."

where the deceased had a permanent job and was  below 40 years.

DEDUCTIONS  "14.

Having considered several subsequent decisions of  this court, we are of the view that where the deceased  was married, the deduction towards personal and living  expenses of the deceased, should be one-third (1/3rd)
 where the number of dependent family members is 2 to  3, one-fourth (1/4th) where the number of dependant  family members is 4 to 6, and one-fifth (1/5th) where  the number of dependent family members exceed six.
 15.
Where the deceased was a bachelor and the  claimants are the parents, the deduction follows a  different principle.

In regard to bachelors, normally,
 50% is deducted as personal and living expenses,
 because it is assumed that a bachelor would tend to  spend more on himself.
Even otherwise, there is also  the possibility of his getting married in a short time, in  which event the contribution to the parent/s and  siblings is likely to be cut drastically.
Further, subject  to evidence to the contrary, the father is likely to have  his own income and will not be considered as a  dependent and the mother alone will be considered as a  dependent.

In the absence of evidence to the contrary,
 brothers and sisters will not be considered as  dependents, because they will either be independent  and earning, or married, or be dependent on the father.

Thus even if the deceased is survived by parents and  siblings, only the mother would be considered to be a  dependent, and 50% would be treated as the personal  and living expenses of the bachelor and 50% as the  contribution to the family.

However, where family of  the bachelor is large and dependent on the income of  the deceased, as in a case where he has a widowed  mother and large number of younger non-earning  sisters or brothers, his personal and living expenses  may be restricted to one-third and contribution to the  family will be taken as two-third."
